Good morning everyone, and thank you for having me here today.
I want to talk about three cases from our gastrointestinal service, and then we will look at a few breast cores at the end.
So the first case is a sixty two year old man who came in with weight loss and a mass in the gastric antrum.
The endoscopist took six biopsies and we received them in formalin the same afternoon.
On low power you can see that the mucosa is replaced by a diffuse infiltrate and there are no well formed glands anywhere in this field.
When we go to high power the cells have abundant intracytoplasmic mucin that pushes the nucleus to one side, which is the classic signet ring cell appearance.
Now this is important because these cells can be very subtle in the lamina propria and they are easy to miss on a busy day.
We ordered a cytokeratin stain and it highlights the single cells infiltrating between the glands.
The diagnosis was poorly cohesive carcinoma, signet ring cell type, and the patient went on to have a total gastrectomy.
In the resection specimen the tumour extended through the muscularis propria into the subserosal tissue.
There was lymphovascular invasion and eight of twenty one lymph nodes contained metastatic carcinoma.
Let me show you the next slide.
Here we have the second case which is a rectal adenocarcinoma treated with neoadjuvant chemoradiation before surgery.
When you look at the deeper wall, the stroma is fibrotic with scattered pools of acellular mucin, and that is typical of therapy.
The question we always ask is whether there are residual viable tumour cells floating in these mucin pools.
In this case we found small clusters of tumour cells at the deep edge so the tumour regression score was two.
Mismatch repair proteins were intact, with nuclear staining for MLH1, PMS2, MSH2 and MSH6 in the tumour cells.
So we called it proficient and the oncologist was happy with that result.
The third case is a little bit different because it comes from the small bowel.
The patient was a forty five year old woman with intermittent abdominal pain and a small submucosal nodule seen on imaging.
Grossly the lesion was firm and yellow and it measured one point two centimetres in greatest dimension.
Microscopically the tumour cells are arranged in nests and trabeculae with a salt and pepper chromatin pattern.
They were positive for synaptophysin and chromogranin, and the Ki-67 proliferation index was about two percent.
So this is a well differentiated neuroendocrine tumour, grade one, according to the current WHO classification.
But I want you to notice the small focus of perineural invasion here at the edge of the slide.
It does not change the grade but it should be mentioned in the report because the surgeons ask about it.
Any questions so far?
Okay, let us move on to the breast cores.
The first breast core contains a bland spindle cell proliferation set in a background of dense collagenous stroma.
The lesional cells expressed desmin and smooth muscle actin but they were negative for keratin and CD34.
We considered a myofibroblastic lesion and we sent the block for molecular testing to exclude other entities.
The second breast core is more straightforward because you can see ductal carcinoma in situ with comedo necrosis in the centre of the ducts.
There is also a small invasive component which measures about three millimetres on this core.
The invasive tumour was estrogen receptor positive in ninety percent of cells and HER2 was negative with a score of one plus.
When the invasive focus is this small we always recommend correlation with the excision specimen.
Next we cut deeper levels of the block and stained them again to look for more invasion.
While we were waiting for the deeper levels the radiologist called and asked whether the calcifications were sampled.
Although the calcifications were present in the specimen radiograph, we only found them in two of the cores.
These details matter because the multidisciplinary team uses them to plan the surgery.
Then we come to the last slide which summarises the key points of today.
First, look carefully at the lamina propria for single cells.
Second, always describe the regression and the residual tumour in resection specimens after neoadjuvant therapy.
Third, report perineural invasion and lymphovascular invasion even when the tumour is small.
And finally, when in doubt, ask a colleague to look at the slide with you.
Thank you very much for your attention.
